issues.issue: "Authorized University official" is undefined, so the class of persons who may demand identification has no stated boundary. The reciprocal duty ("must provide identification if the student requests it") also carries no consequence for non-compliance.

"Replaced as soon as possible" sets no measurable deadline, and the "fee to replace a lost card" is left unquantified. A student's obligation therefore cannot be judged breached on the face of the text.

The parenthetical list of privileges ends in "etc.," a catch-all sitting against enumerated specifics that leaves the covered services indeterminate. "Properly entitled" is likewise undefined and points to no source that fixes entitlement.

"Encouraging, enticing, inuencing or enlisting" — particularly "influencing" — has no boundary, and the prohibition extends to "other ofcial University documents" that are nowhere identified. A student cannot tell from the text which documents or what degree of influence is caught.

Section 2.0 is framed as a shared aspiration ("share the responsibility," "requires the cooperation of all") rather than a rule, leaving open whether it is independently enforceable against a student alongside the specific duties in 2.1–2.13. Its status as preamble versus operative standard is contestable.

The prohibited behaviors in 2.1 — "intimidates," "threatens," "harasses," "invades personal privacy" — are single undefined verbs with no severity, intent, or reasonable-person threshold, so their reach is a matter of construction. "Invades personal privacy" in particular has no stated content anywhere in the document.

The closing sentence of 2.1.f permits campus restriction or emergency suspension of "any student involved in such an incident" pending investigation, which cannot be squared with Section 22.2's rule that a student's status shall not be altered pending final action except for "imminent danger." The two set different triggers for the same interim measure.

"If both parties do not consent" is ambiguous between "if either party does not consent" and "if neither consents," and it presumes exactly two participants. The later edition of the same handbook replaces it with "all parties," confirming the phrase was read as defective.

Section 3.0 as written channels sexual misconduct allegations into the ordinary conduct machinery without saying so, while the 2013–2014 handbook's Section 3.0 expressly directs such allegations to the Special Examiner's Process in Section 22.6 "and not the Student Conduct Process found in Section 19." Which process a student is owed for conduct spanning both editions is left unresolved.

"Sexual contact" is nowhere defined and "explicit consent" is qualified only by "may be considered sexual misconduct," so the provision states no determinate rule of prohibited conduct. The gap between "explicit" consent and consent that is merely "clearly communicated" compounds the uncertainty.

3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" cannot be squared with 3.3, which allows consent to be "communicated verbally or through actions" and lack of consent to be "inferred." One provision demands an express manifestation; the other contemplates inference from conduct.

3.2 makes "taking advantage of someone's incapacitation or intoxication" misconduct, but 3.1 provides that only incapacity — not intoxication — destroys the ability to consent. Read together, 3.2 sanctions sexual activity with a person who under 3.1 is capable of consenting, and "taking advantage" is given no content.

3.3's allowance that consent "may be communicated verbally or through actions" and inferred from circumstances cannot be squared with 3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" for each act of sexual contact. A fact-finder applying both has no rule for consent manifested by conduct in an ongoing relationship.
"Students should report" leaves it unclear whether reporting to Public Safety is a duty enforceable under Section 2.2 or merely advisory. Nothing states the consequence of not reporting.

This provision tells a student only that proceedings "may be initiated" through the DSRCS under Sections 3.1–3.3 and 7, without identifying the adjudicative process, while the 2013–2014 handbook removes those same sections from Section 19 and assigns them to the Special Examiner's Process in Section 22.6. The provision therefore cannot be squared with the process actually applied to Section 3 charges.

This summary states that Section 19.8 "permits the passive assistance of legal counsel," but 19.8 itself says such assistance "may be allowed," i.e., is discretionary and conditioned on consulting SRCS staff. The two descriptions of the same entitlement cannot both be right.

The unqualified promise that "the accuser will be informed of the outcome" conflicts with Section 23.O.2, which says final sanction determinations are communicated to the accused "and in some cases to the accuser." Whether outcome disclosure to a sexual-assault accuser is mandatory or discretionary turns on which controls.

"Any reasonably available changes in academic or living situations" is stated only as staff availability to "assist," with no standard for what changes must be made. Whether this creates any entitlement at all is open.

The Title IX Coordinator is identified by the name of a particular individual and telephone number rather than by office, so the provision is inaccurate the moment the officeholder changes (the later handbook names a different coordinator). Whose office holds the Title IX function is then a matter of construction.

"Highest standards of academic integrity" and "other sanctions" state no ascertainable standard or ceiling, while flatly barring a lack-of-understanding defense. The scope of "work that is falsied or is not the result of the student's own effort" is left to the reader.

The sentence requires work "produced without the assistance of others, except for quotation marks, references, and footnotes" — the stated exception is a set of citation devices, not a form of permitted assistance, so the exception does not fit the rule it qualifies. What assistance is actually permitted cannot be read off the words.

The provision permits faculty-authorized joint work and University tutoring, yet makes providing "one's own work to assist another student" an infringement "either knowingly or through negligence," with no carve-out for the authorized collaboration it has just allowed. The negligence standard has no defined content.
"In identical or similar form" gives no measure of how much similarity converts permissible reuse into an infringement. The advisory second sentence does not supply the missing threshold.

5.0 promises "clear policies" and binds sponsors to "the policies outlined below" and to "guidelines for event sponsorship," but the only subsection that follows in this document is 5.5, and the sponsorship guidelines appear nowhere. What a host has agreed to comply with cannot be determined from the instrument as a whole.

"Other drug paraphernalia" is a catch-all appended to "bongs, pipes," and "abuse of legally-obtained drugs" and "misuse of prescription drugs" are undefined. The reach of the prohibition beyond the enumerated items is a matter of construction.

6.2 makes "inappropriate use of property" a violation without defining it, and 6.1's posting ban is drafted as a specific list closing with "etc." The boundary between prohibited and permitted use is left to the administrator.

The protected-category list ends with the open catch-all "any other category protected by law" and contains the garbled entry "qualied special, disabled veteran," so the classes covered cannot be read off the text. The mangled phrase is repeated inconsistently in 7.1 and 7.3.

Harassment is defined by the "purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering" with education or work, or conduct that "otherwise adversely affects" opportunities, with no severity, pervasiveness, or reasonable-person limit. The definition on its face reaches a single subjectively unwelcome act.

The protected-class list in 7.1 ("gender") differs from 7.0 ("gender identity and expression") and from 7.3 ("gender expression"), and 7.3 alone purports to define the defined term "protected class status." Which list governs a charge under Section 7 cannot be settled from one provision.

The bulleted examples — "unwelcome sexual conduct... including offensive comments, touching" and "comments... that would otherwise tend to be degrading" — are introduced by "includes, but is not limited to" and carry no severity threshold. What conduct actually violates the policy is therefore indeterminate.

It is unclear whether the listed examples are independently sanctionable or must also satisfy 7.1's requirement of an intimidating, hostile, or offensive environment that unreasonably interferes with education or work. The two provisions must be read together to know what is prohibited.

The list is expressly "not an exhaustive list," determinations are made "on a case-by-case basis," and the University reserves power to act on conduct "it deems to be inappropriate" regardless of law. No ascertainable standard of prohibited conduct survives those qualifiers.

"In good faith" is the only limit on the protected act and is undefined, and "corrective action up to and including dismissal" states no gradation. Whether a complainant later found to have exaggerated is protected is left open.

"Falsied a claim" is undefined and the provision specifies no process or standard for that determination, sitting uneasily beside 7.4's protection of good-faith complainants. A complaint found unsubstantiated and one found fabricated are not distinguished.

7.6 directs complaints against students to the Office of the Dean of Student Life, while Section 18.0 provides that disciplinary action may be implemented "only though referral of a violation" to the DSRCS. The two routes for the same complaint are not reconciled.

"Other non-University related purposes" is a general catch-all appended to "commercial, political," leaving the prohibited purposes undefined. The cross-reference to Section 13 points to material not set out with this provision.

The provision opens with a historical recital about the 1947 name change that has no operative effect, and a party could argue it colours or limits the permission that follows. The operative grant is confined to "recognized" organizations, leaving unrecognized groups' use unaddressed by negative implication.

The permission is "subject to the standards and policies published elsewhere in this Handbook," without identifying them, and the facilities-use rules referenced are not reproduced. What conditions attach to the permission cannot be determined without material outside the provision.

17.1's guarantee that room and office privacy "must be respected" stands against 17.3, which authorizes periodic staff inspections of residence hall rooms in the student's absence. Whether 17.1 confers any right the University itself is bound by depends on reading the two together.

The search safeguards are made subject to an exception "as outlined in Section 10.5," a section not set out in this document, so the scope of the exception swallowing the rule is unascertainable. The routine inspections authorized by 17.3 also proceed without any statement of permission.

17.3 permits inspections "to check for illegal possession of University-owned property" on 24 hours' public notice, which is a search in substance and cannot easily be squared with 17.2's requirement of advance individualized written permission specifying the rooms and purpose. The line between an "inspection" and a "search" is not drawn.

Access rights are governed by an external "Brandeis University Records Policy" incorporated by reference, whose terms are not in the handbook and may not match the retention and destruction rules in 19.5 and 19.14. Which document controls a student's access to conduct records is unresolved.

The gatekeeping standards — reports "in a timely manner," "insufcient evidence," "the case lacks merit" — are undefined and committed to the administrator's unreviewable judgment. "Timely" fixes no limitation period at all.

18.0 provides that disciplinary action "may be implemented only though referral of a violation" to the DSRCS, which cannot be squared with Sections 22.3 and 22.4, under which the Dean may indefinitely suspend or dismiss a student with no DSRCS referral and with Section 19 expressly inapplicable. The word "only" is contradicted elsewhere in the instrument.

The mediated outcome is said to be "agreed-upon, recorded, nal, and binding," yet 18.2 provides that failure to adhere may expose the party to further mediation or referral to the conduct process. Finality in 18.1 and the continuing exposure in 18.2 cannot both be given full effect.

"Respect of parameters found in Section 21" is garbled and does not identify what limits Section 21 imposes on a negotiated outcome. "Impasse or other impediment" and "educational benet" likewise give the Director an unmeasured discretion.

The record of a mediated outcome is made subject to "the maintenance provisions in Section 19.5," but 19.5 by its terms governs records of administrative action following a finding of responsibility. Whether a mediated, non-disciplinary record is retained and counted as "conduct action" is not answered.

The provision deems a student's silence for 48 hours after "delivery" — including to a campus mailbox or home address — to be "an acceptance of responsibility for the violation," without requiring actual receipt or defining "extenuating circumstances." Responsibility is thereby established by default rather than by evidence.

Where a student fails to choose, 19.1 directs the administrator to "proceed to sanctioning in accordance with Section 19.3," but 19.3 addresses only a student who has chosen administrative action and then missed a meeting. The cross-reference does not supply the sanctioning procedure it invokes.

19.2 defines "class days" to include final exams and Senior Week and to exclude summer instruction, while 19.6 defines the excluded "Summer" differently and adds Study Abroad periods. The same deadline term carries two definitions in adjacent provisions.

Whether a student's absence was "through no fault of her/his own" is left entirely to the same administrator who decides the case, with no criteria stated. The single-reschedule right is thus unmeasurable on the face of the text.

"Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter dependent upon the conduct of the accused student" states no criterion and no decision-maker, and it is unclear whether charges survive the 90-day cap. The sentence can be read either as a promise of dismissal or as unfettered discretion.

The five-year retention rule is stated twice with different triggers — "from the date of the case outcome" and "from the date of the last conduct action involving that student" — and then subjected to an undefined exception for "extraordinary cases as dened by the Dean." The actual retention period cannot be computed from the words.
